title: Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights
gist: Ars' October research roundup: faster loss of LINE1 'jumping gene' methylation explains why big dogs age faster, Northwestern physicists held a single positron for months, and UV-revealed PhotoTat tattoo inks were developed. It also covers a Westminster skeleton identified as a medieval abbot, new evidence on how Botticelli's model died, and forensic astronomy dating Starry Night to July 22, 1889.

insights.claim: Arizona State University scientists found, using DNA methylation data from 864 dogs in the Dog Aging Project, that giant breeds lose roughly 35 percent more LINE1 jumping-gene methylation per year than small breeds, which links size to faster aging.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The work identifies an epigenetic aging target relevant to longevity research.

insights.claim: Northwestern physicists led by Gerald Gabrielse trapped a single positron for months, keeping it in its quantum ground state at 300 millikelvins, a first step toward precisely measuring its magnetic moment.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Better control of quantum states feeds into precision measurement technology.

insights.claim: Gabrielse says that if the positron's magnetic properties differ from the electron's, contrary to the Standard Model, it would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century.
